title: Analog signals
summary: Values instead of on/off: how a module turns a current or voltage into a number.
objectives: Explain the raw value of an analog input

sections.heading: Continuous values
sections.body: Analog signals represent a quantity continuously: a level, pressure or speed. The module measures a current (for example 4-20 mA) or a voltage (0-10 V) and converts it into an integer, the **raw value**.

sections.heading: Signal to raw value
sections.body: Each platform uses its own number range.
sections.diagram:
0 %  ... 50 % ... 100 %  (process)
  4 mA ... 12 mA ... 20 mA (signal)
  0    ... 5000  ... 10000 (PLC Lab generic raw)
  0    ... 13824 ... 27648 (S7 nominal raw)

sections.heading: Reading the raw value
sections.body: LevelRaw is an INT from the analog module.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: Comparing raw values with engineering numbers (`LevelRaw > 80` meaning 80 %). Always know the raw range of your module and platform.

sections.heading: Compute
sections.body: Use the PLC Lab generic range.

question.question: With 0..10000 for 0..100 %, what raw value is 25 %?

sections.heading: See the raw value
sections.body: On the tank station, watch LevelRaw in Variables while the tank fills.

sections.heading: Summary and troubleshooting note
sections.body:
Analog modules convert currents and voltages into raw integers whose range depends on the platform.

**Troubleshooting note:** Before suspecting the program, compare the measured signal at the terminal with the raw value in the PLC.

checkpoint.question: What is the raw value?
options: The integer delivered by the module
checkpoint.explanation: Scaling turns it into engineering units.

checkpoint.question: Which is a common analog signal?
checkpoint.explanation: 4-20 mA is the classic process signal.
